title: How To Help Difficult Students Who Act Out Due To Emotional Turmoil ue-to-emotional-turmoil/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin discusses students whose misbehavior stems from emotional turmoil rooted in a difficult home life—abuse, poverty, neglect, or substance use—and argues that typical hurtful teacher responses like yelling only compound their pain. He describes the ideal classroom as a shelter: clean and organized to provide a sense of order, anchored by genuine rapport that doesn't take misbehavior personally, and structured by a fair classroom management plan that holds students accountable without judgment or lectures. He emphasizes that sharp routines and clear expectations offer a therapeutic sense of purpose and predictability. The piece closes on a hopeful note, arguing these students are not lost causes but capable of healing and thriving given consistent stability.
points: Misbehavior in many difficult students originates in genuine emotional trauma at home—abuse, poverty, neglect, or substance use—not defiance for its own sake.
A clean, organized classroom environment provides a calming, physical representation of order these students often lack at home.
Rapport built on not taking misbehavior personally, paired with humor and warmth, gives teachers leverage to influence behavior without adding to a student's pain.
A fair, judgment-free classroom management plan should be the sole source of accountability, since lectures and scoldings compound emotional harm.
Sharp routines and clear expectations provide a therapeutic sense of purpose and predictability that can support real healing over time.
quotes: Many difficult students behave the way they do because they’ve experienced—and often continue to experience—emotional turmoil associated with a deplorable home life.
To reach them, your classroom must be a shelter in the midst of the storm.
It has a calming effect that makes them feel safe and valued. Done right, their shoulders will drop when they enter your classroom, their very seat becoming a refuge.
Finger-wagging lectures, dressing downs, sarcastic remarks, and other signs of taking misbehavior personally only work against you and add to their emotional pain.
Rather, with the right classroom management approach, they can begin to heal. They can begin to see themselves and their future in a different light.
